This paper proposes an in-place FFT technique for reducing memory usage during neural network training. It overcomes the dimension mismatch of standard FFTs by using an interesting memory layout, that enables in-place computation. The paper considers the application of parameter-efficient fine-tuning of LLMs using circulant-structured parameter matrices (which requires performing FFT and IFFT in the forward pass). The paper shows the proposed technique is effective in reducing the memory usage in this application.

The paper has received positive reviews overall.  I agree with the reviewers that the proposed technique is novel, useful to the community, and can have broad applications. That being said, the proposed technique is primarily geared towards low memory settings, and is not necessarily optimized for throughput and/or latency. There are also some concerns around lack of quality metrics in the experimental evaluation. The authors addressed these limitations in their rebuttal. I urge the authors to add this discussion to the camera ready version of the paper (in particular the shortcomings of the proposed technique).

Thank you for the thorough and thoughtful rebuttal. Your clarifications and new data address many of my concerns and reflect genuine engagement with the review.

**Performance optimisation**

• Please include preliminary benchmarking results for the planned rdFFT kernel refactor, such as reduced thread synchronisation or improved memory access patterns. Empirical speed-up on representative 1k- and 4k-point FFTs would provide convincing evidence of performance gains.

**FP8 extension**

**Additional accuracy experiments**

• Adding GSM8K evaluation to the final manuscript would further enhance the credibility and completeness of the paper.

I believe that addressing these points in the final manuscript will resolve the outstanding issues on speed, FP8 support, and statistical validation, and will significantly strengthen the paper’s contribution.

Reviewer XryJ.

>● What is the end-to-end training throughput of LLaMA-2-7B compared with full-fine tuning, LoRA, and rFFT?

Thank you very much for your thoughtful question and for taking the time to review our work.
We sincerely appreciate your comments regarding training throughput, and we completely understand your concern. Our work primarily focuses on in-place FFT operator optimization, aiming to significantly reduce memory consumption during training, especially in memory-constrained environments such as single A800 GPUs.

While improving end-to-end training throughput is not the main objective of our method, we acknowledge its practical importance and therefore report the following token-level throughput (measured in tokens per second) on LLaMA-2-7B using the GSM8K dataset. All experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA A800 GPU to reflect realistic deployment scenarios.

Token Throughput (tokens/sec)
| Method           | p    | Token Throughput |
|------------------|------|------------------|
| Full fine-tuning | —    | 3292.45          |
| LoRA (r=32)      | —    | 3361.64          |
| Circulant-FFT    | 512  | 1450.63          |
| Circulant-rFFT   | 512  | 1773.23          |
| Circulant (ours) | 512  | 918.75           |
| Circulant-FFT    | 1024 | 1445.77          |
| Circulant-rFFT   | 1024 | 1768.82          |
| Circulant (ours) | 1024 | 934.60           |
| Circulant-FFT    | 4096 | 1446.98          |
| Circulant-rFFT   | 4096 | 1766.08          |
| Circulant (ours) | 4096 | 933.82           |

As the results indicate, our method currently does not achieve the highest throughput. However, we would like to respectfully emphasize that our contributions are at the operator level, focusing on a memory-efficient in-place implementation. The fine-tuning strategy — block-circulant adaptation — is adopted from prior work (Block Circulant Adapter for Large Language Models, 2025), and is used here solely to demonstrate the practical integration of our operator into real training pipelines.

In terms of GPU memory usage, our method offers significant advantages by eliminating all intermediate buffer allocations during both the forward and backward passes. This results in substantial memory savings, which are especially valuable when training large-scale models under tight hardware constraints.

To better isolate and understand the runtime behavior of the operator itself, we also benchmarked the standalone operator runtime (in milliseconds) of different FFT variants on the A800 GPU:

Operator Runtime (ms)
| Size | fft     | rfft    | rdfft(ours) | ifft    | irfft   | irdfft(ours) |
|------|---------|---------|---------------|---------|---------|----------------|
| 512  | 0.024624 | 0.019496 | 0.027874      | 0.032526 | 0.045015 | 0.023314       |
| 1024 | 0.024908 | 0.019711 | 0.031927      | 0.032214 | 0.042115 | 0.027153       |
| 4096 | 0.025171 | 0.019912 | 0.068703      | 0.032698 | 0.047035 | 0.050319       |

 While the current implementation is not yet optimized for speed, particularly for larger sizes such as 4096, the fully in-place nature of our method remains its most compelling feature. Specifically:

* At smaller sizes (512 and 1024), our method achieves relatively competitive performance, benefiting from reduced synchronization cost.

* At larger sizes, the CUDA thread block size limitation imposes overhead, as our design requires synchronization both within and across blocks. We plan to address this in future work through kernel restructuring and improved scheduling.

* Our inverse transform is faster than the forward one, as it directly reuses the butterfly structure in reverse, resulting in fewer dependencies and better execution efficiency.

We humbly acknowledge that there is still room for improvement in throughput performance. Nonetheless, we believe that the notable memory savings, combined with the in-place execution capability, make our method a meaningful step toward scalable and memory-efficient training — especially for deployment on resource-constrained devices.

We have also provided additional discussion on runtime efficiency in our response to Reviewer Boyr for your reference.

Thank you again for your valuable feedback.

>● Please report validation accuracy/F1 for MRPC and GSM8K under full fine-tuning, LoRA, rFFT-circulant, and rdFFT-circulant.

Thank you very much for raising this important point regarding the learning efficacy of our method.
Our approach is fundamentally a computational and storage-level improvement that reformulates the FFT operator to support truly in-place execution, without changing its mathematical definition. Since no information is discarded in the process, the transform remains theoretically equivalent to standard implementations like rFFT.

To verify this, we conducted operator-level correctness tests, comparing our method with standard FFT on numerical error analysis: 

FFT numerical test

| Input Size | rFFT (Abs / Rel Error)   | Our Method (Abs / Rel Error) |
|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------|
| 512        | 1.88e-07 / 0.0001         | 5.99e-07 / 0.0008             |
| 1024       | 1.92e-07 / 0.0001         | 5.75e-07 / 0.0005             |
| 4096       | 2.55e-07 / 0.0012         | 5.84e-07 / 0.0018             |


The results show that the absolute and relative errors remain at the level of floating-point numerical noise. 

To further evaluate end-to-end fine-tuning effectiveness, we conducted experiments on MRPC, a widely used benchmark for natural language understanding. We compare our method against full fine-tuning, LoRA, and rFFT-based circulant tuning. The results for full fine-tuning, LoRA, and Circulant-rFFT are reproduced from the original paper “Block Circulant Adapter for Large Language Models (2025),” while we newly report the accuracy of our method (in-place Circulant-FFT). All experiments were repeated across multiple seeds for consistency.

MRPC Accuracy (%)

| Method                         | Accuracy (%)        |
|--------------------------------|---------------------|
| Full fine-tuning (FF)          | 90.9                |
| LoRA (r=8, FFT variant)        | 90.2 ± 1.0          |
| Circulant-rFFT (p=512)         | 90.7 ± 1.0          |
| Circulant-rFFT (p=1024)        | 89.7 ± 0.7          |
| Circulant (ours, p=512)        | 90.05 ± 0.9         |
| Circulant (ours, p=1024)       | 90.3 ± 0.7          |

As shown, our method achieves accuracy comparable to both standard rFFT and full fine-tuning, while also offering significant memory savings due to its in-place computation. This supports our claim that the proposed operator can act as a drop-in replacement in training pipelines without sacrificing task performance.

Due to the high computational cost and resource requirements of end-to-end training on LLaMA2-7B with GSM8K, we have not yet included GSM8K fine-tuning results. However, we fully agree with the importance of this evaluation, and we plan to include it in a future preprint version or upon request.

We have also addressed similar accuracy-related points in our responses to Reviewer jHnP and Reviewer 8gGn, which we hope may provide additional context.

> ● Modern GPUs expose E4M3/E5M2 Tensor-Core paths. Can your in-place layout be extended to FP8, and what would be the numerical-stability considerations?

 This is an excellent question, thank you for raising it.
Our current rdFFT implementation is optimized for CUDA cores and supports both FP32 and BF16 natively. Extending rdFFT to support FP8 formats (such as E4M3 and E5M2) is indeed feasible and aligns well with our long-term objective of developing highly memory- and bandwidth-efficient FFT operators.

While native FP8 computation is not yet integrated into our current kernel, we note the following points:

●The in-place memory layout of rdFFT is fully compatible with FP8 storage formats. Within the kernel, data can be temporarily cast to higher precision formats (e.g., FP16 or BF16) for intermediate computations, before being cast back to FP8 for storage. This mixed-precision approach can balance efficiency and numerical accuracy.

●For leveraging Tensor Core FP8 acceleration, the Cooley–Tukey FFT algorithm can be reformulated as a series of matrix multiplications. Prior work such as tcFFT: A Fast Half-Precision FFT Library for NVIDIA Tensor Cores demonstrates this approach. Since rdFFT is based on the same algorithmic principles, our in-place scheme could naturally be adapted to this matrix multiplication formulation to exploit Tensor Cores.

Of course, numerical stability under FP8 precision requires careful evaluation, especially due to the limited dynamic range and increased quantization noise. However, the symmetry-preserving and conjugate-symmetric properties inherent to rdFFT’s output layout provide a solid foundation for applying quantization-aware adjustments and error mitigation techniques.

We consider this an exciting and promising direction for future research, particularly as FP8 hardware becomes more prevalent in AI accelerators. We look forward to exploring this extension to further enhance memory and compute efficiency.

**We thank you again for your valuable suggestion. We will make sure to highlight the validation results and their implications more clearly in our revised manuscript.**

> 1. Can the authors provide a full evaluation of the finetuned models' quality? Specifically, do performance numbers remain on par, or do they drop due to information loss?

Thank you for raising this important question regarding the quality and accuracy of models fine-tuned using rdFFT.
We would like to clarify that rdFFT introduces no information loss due to its design principles. Specifically, rdFFT leverages the conjugate symmetry property of the real-input FFT spectrum: for an input of size N, the FFT output contains only N/2+1 unique complex values. Our method stores these unique values by carefully separating the real and imaginary parts into designated positions within the original buffer, preserving the conjugate symmetric structure. For instance, the DC component (index 0) and the Nyquist frequency component (index N/2) are purely real and handled accordingly to avoid approximation errors.

To quantify the numerical fidelity of rdFFT at the operator level, we measured absolute and relative errors against PyTorch’s standard rfft implementation across different input sizes:

FFT numerical test
| Input Size | rfft (abs/rel error)   | rdfft (abs/rel error)  |
|------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| 512        | 1.88e-07 (0.0001)      | 5.99e-07 (0.0008)      |
| 1024       | 1.92e-07 (0.0001)      | 5.75e-07 (0.0005)      |
| 4096       | 2.55e-07 (0.0012)      | 5.84e-07 (0.0018)      |

These errors are negligible and demonstrate that rdFFT faithfully reproduces the spectral results.

Furthermore, we evaluated the end-to-end task performance by fine-tuning models on the MRPC benchmark, a standard NLU dataset:

| Method                     | MRPC Accuracy (%) |
|----------------------------|-------------------|
| Full fine-tuning (FF)       | 90.9              |
| LoRA (r=8, FFT variant)     | 90.2 ± 1.0        |
| Circulant-rFFT (p=512)      | 90.7 ± 1.0        |
| Circulant-rFFT (p=1024)     | 89.7 ± 0.7        |
| Circulant-rdFFT (p=512)     | 90.05 ± 0.9       |
| Circulant-rdFFT (p=1024)    | 90.3 ± 0.7        |

The results confirm that rdFFT maintains task-level accuracy on par with both standard rFFT-based tuning and full-precision fine-tuning. This strongly indicates that our in-place FFT design does not degrade model quality or learning efficacy.

Related discussions on model accuracy and validation can also be found in our responses to Reviewer XryJ and Reviewer jHnP.

In summary, both numerical evaluation and downstream task performance validate that rdFFT functions correctly without sacrificing accuracy or introducing information loss. We will clarify these points further in the final manuscript. Thank you again for your valuable feedback.

> 2. Given that the motivation for in-place FFT stems from vision tasks beyond 1D, how could the proposed approach be extended to 2D, 3D, or nD settings? Does the inherent split of real and imaginary parts preclude such extensions?

Thank you very much for this insightful and important question. 
Our core contribution is an in-place layout and kernel for the 1D Cooley–Tukey FFT, optimized for real inputs. However, the method is not limited to 1D: multi-dimensional FFTs (2D, 3D, etc.) are typically implemented as batched 1D FFTs along each axis, and this principle remains applicable to our rdFFT.

● The memory layout and conjugate structure generalize cleanly across dimensions.

● We have tested the building blocks needed to support higher-dimensional transforms using separable 1D passes.

● The butterfly computation and symmetry remain valid, and our in-place logic can be adapted accordingly.

We appreciate the reviewer’s question regarding the numerical accuracy and end-to-end performance of our proposed method.
To verify the correctness of rdFFT, we conducted both operator-level numerical comparisons and downstream task evaluations.
The results show that the absolute and relative errors remain at the level of floating-point numerical noise 

FFT numerical test
| Input Size | rfft (abs/rel error)   | rdfft (abs/rel error)  |
|------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| 512        | 1.88e-07 (0.0001)      | 5.99e-07 (0.0008)      |
| 1024       | 1.92e-07 (0.0001)      | 5.75e-07 (0.0005)      |
| 4096       | 2.55e-07 (0.0012)      | 5.84e-07 (0.0018)      |

Despite its in-place and memory-efficient design, rdFFT exhibits numerical accuracy comparable to standard rFFT, with errors remaining within acceptable bounds for practical deep learning use. These results confirm that rdFFT is a reliable drop-in replacement for real-input FFT computations.

End-to-end Task Accuracy (MRPC benchmark):
To further validate practical applicability, we evaluated rdFFT in a circulant fine-tuning setting on the MRPC task, comparing it against full fine-tuning and rFFT-based approaches: 

| Method                     | MRPC Accuracy (%) |
|----------------------------|-------------------|
| Full fine-tuning (FF)       | 90.9              |
| LoRA (r=8, FFT variant)     | 90.2 ± 1.0        |
| Circulant-rFFT (p=512)      | 90.7 ± 1.0        |
| Circulant-rFFT (p=1024)     | 89.7 ± 0.7        |
| Circulant-rdFFT (p=512)     | 90.05 ± 0.9       |
| Circulant-rdFFT (p=1024)    | 90.3 ± 0.7        |

The results show that rdFFT achieves task-level performance on par with both rFFT and full fine-tuning, without introducing degradation in learning quality.

In summary, both numerical and downstream task results confirm that rdFFT maintains accuracy while significantly reducing memory usage, supporting its practical use in large-scale training.

Similar concerns regarding accuracy have also been discussed in our responses to Reviewer XryJ and Reviewer 8gGn, which you may refer to for additional context.

> 2. By storing the real and imaginary parts only, is the impact of conjugate reconstruction investigated? such as computational overhead, error sensitivity, etc

 We appreciate this excellent question. Our method adopts the same Hermitian symmetry assumption as conventional rfft implementations, storing only the unique real and imaginary components of the spectrum. The conjugate symmetry is preserved implicitly through the memory layout, eliminating the need for explicit conjugate reconstruction during computation.

●Computational overhead: No additional overhead is introduced. All arithmetic operations (e.g., inverse transforms, gradient computations) are performed directly on the compact, interleaved representation without requiring reconstruction of the full complex spectrum.

●Error sensitivity: Since our design mirrors the reconstruction assumptions of standard rfft, the numerical behavior is equally stable. As shown in our operator-level comparisons (see Q1), the absolute and relative errors remain within the same magnitude as rfft, confirming no added numerical sensitivity.

●Theoretical soundness: Our layout is mathematically consistent with the Cooley–Tukey FFT framework. The structure preserves exact conjugate symmetry across forward and backward passes, and maintains gradient correctness throughout training. This ensures full compatibility with autograd-based optimization workflows.

In summary, rdFFT maintains the same computational and numerical guarantees as existing FFT-based operators, while offering improved memory efficiency and supporting in-place execution with no loss in correctness or precision.

> 1. Could you benchmark on the speed of this operator?

Thank you for raising this important question. While the primary objective of rdFFT is to minimize memory consumption via truly in-place computation, we have also conducted runtime benchmarking to evaluate its practical efficiency.

The table below reports the media runtime (in milliseconds) over 1000 runs on an A800 GPU with FP32 precision, comparing various FFT variants across different input sizes:

| Size | fft     | rfft    | rdfft(ours) | ifft    | irfft   | irdfft(ours) |
|------|---------|---------|---------------|---------|---------|----------------|
| 512  | 0.024624 | 0.019496 | 0.027874      | 0.032526 | 0.045015 | 0.023314       |
| 1024 | 0.024908 | 0.019711 | 0.031927      | 0.032214 | 0.042115 | 0.027153       |
| 4096 | 0.025171 | 0.019912 | 0.068703      | 0.032698 | 0.047035 | 0.050319       |

As shown, rdFFT does not outperform existing real-valued FFT implementations in terms of speed, especially at larger sizes. This is expected and stems from our core design choice: truly in-place computation that avoids any additional memory allocation. Such a design favors memory savings over raw throughput and is particularly beneficial in large-scale or memory-constrained scenarios.

For smaller sizes (e.g., 512 and 1024), rdFFT achieves comparable performance to rFFT, demonstrating that in-place computation can be efficient when the number of synchronization points remains low. However, for larger sizes like 4096, the runtime increases due to the limitation on the number of threads within a CUDA thread block. In our implementation, synchronization is required not only within blocks (for in-block butterfly stages), but also across blocks, which incurs additional overhead.

It’s also worth noting that our inverse rdFFT is slightly faster than the forward version. This is because our inverse transform directly reuses the structure of the forward butterfly computation in reverse order, benefiting from fewer data dependencies.

In future work, we plan to optimize inter-block synchronization and explore adaptive scheduling strategies to further improve the runtime while preserving our key advantage of in-place execution.

Relevant insights on runtime efficiency are also addressed in our response to Reviewer XryJ, which we invite you to review.

> 2. Could you discuss more on the kernel tuning results if possible (to see whether this operator fits a large range of matrix sizes)?

Thank you for this valuable and insightful question.
To ensure that rdFFT performs efficiently across a wide range of input sizes, particularly those encountered in large-scale models such as LLaMA2-7B, we have incorporated kernel-level tuning and multiple implementation strategies.

In transformer architectures, the input to the QKV projection layers is often reshaped into 4D tensors with shape [B, C, R, D], where D (the hidden dimension) typically serves as the dimension over which FFT is applied. In practical settings, D frequently takes values such as 512, 1024, and 4096, corresponding to different model scales and attention head configurations.

To adapt to these varying sizes, we conduct empirical tuning of the kernel configuration, especially the threads-per-block parameter, as follows:

●For D = 512, we find that 256 threads per block yields a good balance between occupancy and memory throughput.

●For D = 1024, using 512 threads per block ensures efficient shared memory usage and coalesced access, while maintaining high parallelism.

●For D = 4096, 1024 threads per block provides near-optimal utilization of the A100 GPU's computational resources, while keeping register and shared memory usage within hardware limits.

Furthermore, we implement two distinct kernel designs to accommodate different workload scales:

1.***Single-pass kernel design:***
This version executes the entire transform in a single kernel call without requiring global memory synchronization between stages. It minimizes kernel launch overhead and is particularly effective for small to medium-sized transforms (e.g., D = 512, 1024), where the FFT stages fit well within a single thread block's resource envelope.

2.***Multi-stage kernel design:***
For larger dimensions (e.g., D = 4096), we employ a staged computation strategy that decomposes the transform into multiple kernel launches. This approach improves control flow simplicity, reduces register pressure, and enhances memory access locality, resulting in better performance and scalability on large inputs.

These kernel strategies, combined with manual tuning, make rdFFT adaptable to a broad spectrum of tensor sizes in modern deep learning models. While our core motivation lies in minimizing memory footprint via true in-place computation, we fully acknowledge the importance of runtime performance and general applicability. To that end, we are currently exploring automatic kernel configuration selection and adaptive autotuning mechanisms as part of our future work.

> Weaknesses: As I understand, this method only supports matrix sizes of powers of 2, which may limit the scope of it as many layers in modern LLMs are not of those sizes.

Thank you for pointing out this concern.
We would like to clarify that although our method is designed to optimize Butterfly-based FFT computation, it is not limited to input sizes that are powers of 2.

Similar to standard FFT libraries (e.g., cuFFT), our implementation supports non-power-of-two input lengths via zero-padding and Butterfly decomposition generalization. The underlying idea of rdFFT focuses on improving the in-place computation and memory efficiency of the Butterfly operations themselves. Since the Butterfly pattern can be applied to any input size through padding or factorization into mixed-radix stages, rdFFT remains applicable to arbitrary input dimensions, including those frequently found in modern LLM layers.

In practice, many transformer layers (e.g., attention projections with dimensions such as 768, 1024, or 3072) can be efficiently handled by our implementation using minimal padding when necessary, with negligible impact on runtime or memory usage.
Therefore, we believe that this limitation does not fundamentally restrict the applicability of our method, and we will make this point clearer in the final version of the paper. Thank you again for raising this important clarification opportunity.

**Thank you for your comprehensive review and valuable suggestions. We hope our responses clarify your concerns and demonstrate the contributions of our work.**

summary.value: This paper introduces rdFFT, a real-domain, in-place Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) framework intended to reduce memory use in neural network training. The method uses butterfly operation symmetry and conjugate properties to create an implicit complex encoding scheme that operates within the original real-valued memory buffer. This approach is designed to address the memory-space mismatch in standard real FFT (rFFT) implementations. The paper reports that experiments on RoBERTa-large and LLaMA2-7B show reductions in peak memory usage compared to other FFT methods and LoRA.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1. The paper proposes what it claims is the first truly in-place FFT operator for real-valued data that resolves the input-output dimension mismatch of standard rFFT, contributing at the level of a fundamental arithmetic operator.

2. The authors validate the method with both isolated single-layer analyses and full-model fine-tuning on large-scale models (LLaMA2-7B and RoBERTa-large), providing a breakdown of memory usage.

3. The proposed rdFFT is benchmarked against standard complex FFT, rFFT in both full fine-tuning and LoRA. The paper's results indicate lower memory usage compared to these methods under the tested conditions.

4. The implementation include BF16, which is important in modern LLMs while lacks proper implementation in traditional FFT libraries.

Weaknesses:

1. As I understand, this method only supports matrix sizes of powers of 2, which may limit the scope of it as many layers in modern LLMs are not of those sizes.

2. Another important aspect, training speed, is not properly discussed in this paper.

summary.value: The paper proposes rdFFT, a real-domain fully in-place fast Fourier transform operator for neural-network training. By interleaving the N + 2 real outputs of a conventional real-input FFT back into the original N slots and proving that this layout is preserved throughout the Cooley–Tukey computation, rdFFT performs both forward and backward passes without extra memory movement. A succinct CUDA kernel with native bf16 and FP16 support eliminates copy and padding operations, lowers peak GPU memory by roughly 25~30\% versus rFFT, and keeps throughput within three percent on LLaMA-2-7B and RoBERTa-Large fine-tuning tasks running on a single A100 80 GB GPU, offering a lossless operator-level alternative that can complement or precede parameter-efficient adaptation methods.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
## Strength
- Operator-level novelty: The interleaved layout compresses N + 2 real slots into N and is accompanied by a rigorous symmetry proof. 
- True in-place execution: Both forward FFT and backward IFFT run without auxiliary buffers, including gradient overwrite. 
- bf16 support: Existing cuFFT/FFTW kernels lack bf16; rdFFT supports it natively. 

## Weakness
- No accuracy metrics: The paper assumes “lossless” equivalence but never reports validation accuracy/F1 on MRPC, GSM8K or any task, leaving the practical impact unverified.
- No throughput metrics: The paper never discloses latency or training throughput, which seriously limits the practical relevance of the method. 
- No FP8 support: While the implementation covers FP32 and bfloat16, it does not support the FP8 formats now available on Hopper/Blackwell-class GPUs, leaving potential memory- and bandwidth gains untapped.

questions.value:
- What is the end-to-end training throughput of LLaMA-2-7B compared with full-fine tuning, LoRA, and rFFT?
- Please report validation accuracy/F1 for MRPC and GSM8K under full fine-tuning, LoRA, rFFT-circulant, and rdFFT-circulant.
- Modern GPUs expose E4M3/E5M2 Tensor-Core paths. Can your in-place layout be extended to FP8, and what would be the numerical-stability considerations?

While a few areas—such as performance optimisation and FP8 extension—still require further development, the authors have laid out a reasonable and credible plan for addressing them in the final version. I also believe that including GSM8K evaluation will further improve the completeness of the work. Overall, the paper has improved in clarity and depth, and I have decided to raise my rating based on this improved assessment.

summary.value:
This paper is introducing an in-place FFT framework that can be used in deep learning with reducing memory. The main contribution from the authors include 1.The rdFFT, a real-valued, fully in-place Fourier transform operator that eliminates memory space mismatches, offering improved practicality and usability for neural network applications compared to existing libraries. 2. A new memory layout design, develop a novel butterfly execution scheme for IFFT computation, and provide support for the bfloat16 data type. 3. Authors have integrated the proposed rdFFT into neural network models via circulant-structured parameter matrix and validate on real-world models. 
The experimental results show the proposed method significantly reduces memory consumption.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The paper presents a novel in-place Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) operations for model training through the use of circulant-
structured parameter matrices, which have shown a significant memory reducing compared with other fft libraries. The method enables fully in-place FFT computation for real-valued input, with zero memory overhead and compatible with the Cooley–Tukey algorithm.
2. The submission demonstrates a strong technical foundation with a robust experimental design and clear evidence supporting the claims presented in the paper. The experiments include different settings with the comprehensive memory analysis.
3. The paper is well-structured and clearly written, making it accessible to a broader audience. 
4. This work have offered a promising direction for frequency-domain lightweight adaptation.The proposed method has the potential for wide adoption and could inspire future research in this area.

Weakness:
1. Other than the memory cost, accuracy impact is not fully investigated. Authors would also be curious about the accuracy/error results on the proposed fft operations. 
2. By storing the real and imaginary parts only, the impact of conjugate reconstruction would also provide more proof, such as computational overhead, error sensitivity, etc

questions.value:
1. As well as the promising memory reducing results, is there any numeric accuracy comparision between standard fft, rfft and proposed method? or any end-to-end training result.
2. By storing the real and imaginary parts only, is the impact of conjugate reconstruction investigated? such as computational overhead, error sensitivity, etc

summary.value: The authors propose to learn a new kind of Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on real valued data which is in place and does not require any additional storage during computation making the operation more space efficient. Similar to the FFT, they leverage the recursive approach of a Butterfly graph and divide the computation of the real-valued FFT into subcomputations. However, their resulting frequency representation is only reported in real-valued numbers. Their evaluation showcases reduced memory usage for single layer training and model fine-tuning.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength:
- The proposed approach demonstrates significantly lower memory consumption compared to common FFT methods. This makes it highly relevant given the current trend of large models and input dimensions.
- The proposed approach is interesting and relevant because, with growing model and dataset sizes, the use of frequency representation (e.g., for leveraging the convolution theorem) is becoming more popular. Additionally, the approach inherently lowers memory consumption. 

Weaknesses:
1. The resulting models are evaluated solely on GPU consumption, but a performance evaluation of the finetuned models is missing. Consequently, it is hard to judge the actual functionality, meaning whether the proposed real-valued FFT works as intended. The authors should provide evaluations on the trained models.
2. The applicability remains debatable. While the authors motivate their work with vision applications that leverage the frequency domain for efficient computation and enhanced model learning, the provided implementation appears to function only for 1D signals.
3. Further, the separation into imaginary and real part into different array positions does imply that standard usage like the convolution theorem would need to be adapted. While this is discussed in the paper's limitations, no future strategy for tackling this problem is provided.

questions.value:
1. Can the authors provide a full evaluation of the finetuned models' quality? Specifically, do performance numbers remain on par, or do they drop due to information loss?
2. Given that the motivation for in-place FFT stems from vision tasks beyond 1D, how could the proposed approach be extended to 2D, 3D, or nD settings? Does the inherent split of real and imaginary parts preclude such extensions?
3. What strategies might enable the proposed approach to regain the inherent interaction offered by complex numbers?

limitations.value:
The authors identify their paper's greatest limitation as the split into distinct real and imaginary numbers, which prevents direct use of complex forms. Consequently, as they state in lines 315-316, "additional logic is required to decode the real-valued encoding into a usable complex form."

I hope the authors can elaborate on how to adapt their approach to work like complex values and/or in settings beyond 1D.

Furthermore, while I believe this work is a step in the right direction, a thorough evaluation of the resulting model quality is necessary to judge the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

If the authors manage to address these points, I would be happy to raise my score.

final_justification.value: The authors' rebuttal successfully addressed my concerns, and as a result, I have increased my score. For future work, I would be very interested in seeing this algorithm extended to an nD setting.

title.value: Memory-Efficient Training with In-Place FFT Implementation

abstract.value:
Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT) are widely used to reduce memory and computational costs in deep learning. However, existing implementations, including standard FFT and real FFT (rFFT), cannot achieve true in-place computation. In particular, rFFT maps an input of size $n$ to a complex output of size $\frac{n}{2}+1$, causing dimensional mismatch and requiring additional memory allocation.
We propose the first real-domain, fully in-place FFT framework (rdFFT) that preserves input-output dimensional consistency ($n \rightarrow n$). By leveraging butterfly operation symmetry and conjugate properties in the frequency domain, we design an implicit complex encoding scheme that eliminates intermediate cache usage entirely.
Theoretically, our method reduces memory usage by 50\% compared to rFFTs. Moreover, it enables zero-cache parameter updates by utilizing the derivative property of the Fourier transform to compute matrix inverses efficiently without intermediate storage. Experiments on multiple natural language understanding tasks demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in maintaining model performance while significantly lowering memory overhead, offering a promising direction for frequency-domain lightweight adaptation.
